fetched_contents.text: Peritoneal dialysis first policy in Hong Kong for 35 years: Global impact Abstract Peritoneal dialysis (PD) first policy has been established in Hong Kong since 1985. After 35 years of practice, the PD first policy in Hong Kong has influenced many countries around the world including governments, health ministries, nephrologists and renal nurses on the overall health policy structure and clinical practice in treating kidney failure patients using PD as an important dialysis modality. In 2021, the International Association of Chinese Nephrologists and the Hong Kong Society of Nephrology jointly held a symposium celebrating the 35 years of PD first policy in Hong Kong. In that symposium, experts and opinion leaders from around the world have shared their perspectives on how the PD first policy has grown and how it has affected PD and home dialysis practice globally. The advantages of PD during COVID‐19 pandemic were highlighted and the use of telemedicine as an important adjunct was discussed in treating kidney failure patients to improve the overall quality of care. Barriers to PD and the need for sustainability of PD first policy were also emphasized. Overall, the knowledge awareness of PD as a home dialysis for patients, families, care providers and learners is a prerequisite for the success of PD first. A critical mass of PD regional hubs is needed for training and mentorship. Importantly, the alignment of policy and clinical goals are enablers of PD first program. Keywords: global impact, Hong Kong, PD first policy, peritoneal dialysis Summary at a Glance Thirty five years of practice of peritoneal dialysis (PD) first policy in Hong Kong has influenced many countries around the world including governments, health ministries, nephrologists and renal nurses on the overall health policy structure and clinical practice in treating kidney failure patients using PD as an important dialysis modality. 1. INTRODUCTION Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is an important contributor to morbidity and mortality from non‐communicable diseases. Globally, in 2017, 1.2 million people died from CKD. 1 The major causes of CKD leading to end‐stage kidney disease (ESKD) are diabetes mellitus (DM), glomerular diseases, and hypertension. 2 The epidemic of DM contributes to the major burden of CKD. In 2010, 285 million (6%) of the adult population worldwide had DM and this is projected to increase to 8% in 2030. 2 , 3 Availability of kidney replacement therapy (KRT) makes possible the long‐term application of life‐saving but costly treatment for patients with ESKD. The number of people receiving KRT exceeds 2.5 million and is projected to double to 5.4 million by 2030. 1 Currently, the most common KRT modalities are haemodialysis (HD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD). Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) and automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) at home are effective methods of KRT and were found to be less expensive than in‐centre chronic haemodialysis in most countries. Nowadays, home based dialysis such as PD is considered to be a preferred option particularly under the circumstances of pandemics as COVID‐19. Hong Kong (HK) had carried out intermittent PD therapy since 1969 and now has the highest PD patient proportion around the world, attributed to successful “peritoneal dialysis first” (PD‐First) policy since 1985. 4 35‐years of successful PD practice in HK has made a positive global impact and pushed forward the PD implementation all over the world especially in Asia‐Pacific countries. Starting from early 2000, representatives from Ministries of Health of Thailand and Singapore had visited HK officially to learn the experience of PD First. Throughout these years, the leading nephrologists of Hong Kong have been invited by Ministries of Health from China, Taiwan, Malaysia and Mongolia to share the experience of PD First Policy of Hong Kong. The PD First Policy of Hong Kong with over 70% PD had also been officially complimented by the Secretary of Department of Health and Human Services of USA as exemplary in 2019. This was made when the Secretary was promoting the Executive Order of Advancing American Kidney Health Initiatives: USA wants to ensure 80% of new kidney failure patients in 2025 either are receiving dialysis at home or are receiving a transplant. 2. HISTORY: PD FIRST POLICY IN HK There have been many milestones of KRT in HK from the 60s to 80s. Maintenance HD and intermittent PD were started in 1969 and CAPD was initiated in early 1980s. In the year 1985, a “PD‐First Policy” was introduced by the Central Renal Committee (CRC) of the Medical and Health Department, which was established to help planning and development of KRT provision in HK. The Policy was further promoted by the Hospital Authority (HA) of HK Government to meet with the rising numbers on waiting list for dialysis provision, 5 , 6 as CAPD was shown to be a cost‐effective treatment for ESKD. This policy meant that PD was provided as the first‐line dialysis regimen unless a medical contraindication dictated otherwise. At the start of the PD‐First Policy, all patients put on PD were on CAPD 6 . The official data from other countries such as the United Kingdom 7 showed that limited treatment was being made available for ESKD patients over the same period, and HK took the first step to start CAPD first treatment. Afterwards, APD was gradually introduced into the program and further expanded due to APD machine subsidy provided by charitable organizations from 1997. In HK, the principle is to start CAPD first, with APD reserved for patients with high membrane transport status or compelling psychosocial needs, 5 , 8 as both CAPD and APD have been shown to provide high‐quality dialysis for patients in HK. ## Which dialysis option is better for most patients?

Overall, the evidence suggests that **peritoneal dialysis (PD) is not universally better than in-center hemodialysis (HD), but it can be more suitable for many patients depending on their circumstances**. The strongest conclusion is that **PD and in-center HD are both viable options, but neither should be chosen purely by default** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R3].

### Clinical outcomes comparison: survival, complications, and safety

The evidence indicates that **PD can offer patient survival comparable to or better than in-center HD, while preserving residual kidney function and empowering patient autonomy** [N2-R1]. That is a major advantage for long-term outcomes. However, the evidence also notes important differences in complication profiles. For frail elderly patients, **in-center HD may have advantages in efficient solute removal and limited time spent for treatment**, which is relevant for safety and tolerability in vulnerable patients [N2-R3]. 

On the safety side, the evidence is mixed. One source states that **PD is considered a preferred option particularly under pandemic conditions**, partly because of its home-based nature and reduced need for frequent center visits [N2-R1][N1-F1]. Another source notes that **home dialysis patients are generally younger and healthier than those treated with in-center HD in the US**, implying that patient selection and health status matter substantially for safety and outcomes [N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence does **not support a single modality as universally superior**; instead, it supports the idea that **each modality has strengths and risks depending on the patient population** [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Burden and quality-of-life tradeoffs for patient lifestyle

Quality-of-life and burden considerations are a major part of the evidence. PD is associated with **greater autonomy, lower anxiety, a better relationship with medical staff, and lower pain**, according to one source [N3-R3]. Another source reports that **HD patients report lower quality of life in the environment and social relationships domains**, and more symptoms in the GHQ-28 [N3-R1]. A broader review of burden, health-related quality of life, and employment also supports the idea that PD and HD place different demands on patients and their families [N3-R2][N3-R5].

In practical terms, PD can be **more convenient for travel and mobility**, and patients on PD may experience **continuous dialysis that can improve well-being** [N2-R2]. But PD also requires home-based treatment, which may introduce burdens such as managing dialysate, catheter care, and adherence. HD, by contrast, requires regular trips to the center and more structured time commitments [N2-R2][N3-R1]. So the evidence favors **PD for patients who value flexibility, autonomy, and less disruption to daily life**, while **HD may be more appropriate for patients who prefer structured in-center care** [N2-R2][N3-R3][N3-R1].

### When each option is more suitable based on patient factors

The evidence strongly supports a **patient-centered, individualized approach** rather than a one-size-fits-all rule. A clinical guideline source emphasizes that **non-medical reasons are important factors in dialysis modality selection**, and that **the expertise of the nephrologic team is the most important one** [N5-R3]. Another source says that clinical guidelines recommend **patients' self-selection of KRT modality through shared decision-making**, which requires predialysis education and discussion [N5-R4]. A third source similarly stresses that **modality education is needed for all eligible kidney disease patients** [N5-R5].

So the best fit depends on several patient factors:
- **Age and frailty**: In frail elderly patients, in-center HD may be preferred for more efficient solute removal and less time burden [N2-R3].
- **Mobility and lifestyle**: PD may be more suitable for people who want flexibility, travel, or a more independent routine [N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **Psychosocial support**: PD may be better if the patient has family or caregiver support, whereas HD may be preferred if the patient prefers routine center care [N2-R2][N3-R1].
- **Health status and education**: HD may be more appropriate for older or less healthy patients, while PD may be better for younger, healthier patients who can manage home treatment [N2-R4].
- **Dialysis goals**: PD can preserve residual kidney function, while HD may be preferred for rapid solute clearance in some settings [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Whether evidence favors one modality overall or depends on individual circumstances

The evidence does **not favor one modality overall**. Instead, it clearly favors **individualized decision-making**. One source says that **the appropriateness of the dialysis modality selection process is important**, and that a percentage of patients could potentially have been offered a different modality [N5-R2]. Another says that **non-medical reasons are important factors**, and that **expertise of the nephrologic team is the most important one** [N5-R3]. A third says that **shared decision-making is recommended**, with predialysis education as a minimum requirement [N5-R4].

In short, the evidence supports:
- **PD as a strong first choice for many patients**, especially those who can manage home treatment and benefit from autonomy and flexibility [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **HD as a strong first choice in some patients**, especially frail or elderly patients, where in-center care may be safer or more convenient [N2-R3].
- **A decision based on the patient’s unique medical, psychosocial, and lifestyle factors**, with shared decision-making and education central to the process [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## Bottom line for most patients
The best answer is **not “choose PD” or “choose HD”**. The evidence suggests that **each modality has advantages and disadvantages**, and the better choice depends on the **patient’s age, health status, lifestyle, support system, and preferences** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-R3]. In general, **PD may be better for most patients who can manage home dialysis and value autonomy**, while **HD may be better for frail or elderly patients or those who prefer in-center care** [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-R4].

## What is the current dialysis landscape in Hong Kong?

The evidence shows that Hong Kong has a **very strong PD-first policy** and that **peritoneal dialysis is much more common than hemodialysis**. It also indicates that **home dialysis is supported in practice, but not universally accessible**, and that **local policy, training, and reimbursement structures influence patient choice** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F2][N6-F1].

### Which dialysis modality is more common in Hong Kong

The evidence is clear: **PD is far more common than HD in Hong Kong**. One source says that **in 2013, the ratio of PD to HD was 76.2% to 23.8%**, the highest in the world [N1-R2]. Another source states that **as of 2021, 73.6% of HA dialysis patients were on PD and 26.3% on HD** [N1-F1]. A recent Renal Registry update also reports that **82.3% of new patients received PD and 17.0% received HD in 2022** [N1-F2]. So the current landscape is **PD dominant**.

### How access and support for home dialysis differ from in-center care

Home dialysis, especially PD, is supported in Hong Kong through a structured system. The evidence shows that **Hong Kong has 16 renal centres providing peritoneal dialysis treatment** and that **as of 2021, 15 centres have over 180 PD patients** [N1-R1]. It also states that **the HA has had a PD-first policy since 1985**, and that **PD was provided as the first-line dialysis regimen unless a medical contraindication dictated otherwise** [N1-F1]. This policy structure suggests that **home dialysis is integrated into the broader system**, but not automatically available to every patient.

In contrast, in-center hemodialysis remains a standard option, though less common. The evidence also notes that **the PD-first policy was introduced by the Central Renal Committee and promoted by the Hospital Authority** to meet rising waiting list needs and because CAPD was shown to be cost-effective [N1-F1]. So, access is **not equally distributed** across settings. PD is supported through a policy and training framework, while HD is still available but less emphasized in the current landscape [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Any local reimbursement or policy differences affecting patient choice

The evidence indicates that **policy differences matter**. Hong Kong has a **PD-first policy**, which is a major determinant of patient choice [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The evidence also points to **training and support structures** as important to implementation, including **home dialysis training** and **equipment support** [N6-R2][N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide a complete local reimbursement schedule in the provided excerpts, so this part is only partially supported.

That said, the broader policy context suggests that **reimbursement and reimbursement-related incentives can shape access**. The evidence notes that **home dialysis is considered a preferred option, especially under pandemic conditions**, and that **telemedicine and support structures are important adjuncts** to care [N1-F1]. Another source also says that **policy and clinical goals must align for a PD-first program to succeed**, implying that **system-level incentives are part of the landscape** [N1-F1]. Therefore, while the provided evidence is thin on exact reimbursement details, it does support the conclusion that **policy differences, including PD-first policy and training support, affect patient choice** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R2].

### How long the PD-first policy has been in place and its implementation

The evidence is very clear on this point. The PD-first policy was introduced in **Hong Kong in 1985** by the **Central Renal Committee of the Medical and Health Department** [N1-F1]. It was further promoted by the **Hospital Authority (HA)** to meet rising dialysis waiting list needs [N1-F1]. The policy was based on the idea that CAPD was cost-effective and should be provided first unless there was a medical contraindication [N1-F1].

The implementation has been long-standing and evolving. The evidence says that **starting from early 2000, representatives from Thailand and Singapore visited Hong Kong to learn PD-first experience**, and that **leading Hong Kong nephrologists have shared the policy with countries in Asia-Pacific** [N1-F1]. It also states that the **PD-first policy has been officially complimented by the U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services in 2019** as exemplary [N1-F1]. More recent data show that **the PD proportion has declined slightly from 82% in 2009 to 73.6% in 2021**, partly because of a planned increase in HD provision by the HA [N1-F1]. This indicates that the policy has been **implemented for over 35 years** and continues to evolve in practice [N1-F1][N1-F2].

## Bottom line
In Hong Kong, the current dialysis landscape is dominated by **peritoneal dialysis**, with a strong **PD-first policy that has been in place since 1985** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Access to home dialysis exists through training and support structures, but the evidence does not provide a complete reimbursement picture [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In-center hemodialysis remains available, but it is less common than PD [N1-F1]. Overall, the landscape is shaped by **policy, training, and reimbursement differences**, with PD-first policy being central to patient choice [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-R2].

## Practical considerations for choosing PD or dialysis center in Hong Kong

Choosing between PD and dialysis center care in Hong Kong involves four main practical considerations: **availability of home dialysis training and equipment support**, **travel and time commitments for dialysis center visits**, **cost and insurance coverage implications**, and **local policy or system barriers to starting home dialysis** [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

### Availability of home dialysis training and equipment support

Training and equipment support are central to starting PD. The evidence shows that **Hong Kong has 16 renal centres providing PD treatment**, and that **as of 2021, 15 centres have over 180 PD patients** [N1-R1]. It also states that **the HA has had a PD-first policy since 1985**, and that **PD was provided as the first-line dialysis regimen unless a medical contraindication dictated otherwise** [N1-F1]. That suggests a well-established training and support infrastructure.

The evidence also supports the importance of **pre-start training**. A National Kidney Foundation source says that **before starting home dialysis, the training team checks the home, sets up the treatment space, arranges needed surgery, and provides information on dialysis** [N6-R2]. Another source says that **training programs vary in length depending on the patient’s needs** and teach patients how to safely perform dialysis, monitor health, and manage complications [N6-R5]. This indicates that **Hong Kong’s system likely supports training**, though the provided evidence does not specify whether all patients receive the same level of support.

### Travel and time commitments for dialysis center visits

For dialysis center care, the main burden is **travel and time**. The evidence notes that **PD is preferred under pandemic conditions because of reduced need for frequent center visits** [N2-R1][N1-F1]. In contrast, HD requires regular trips to the dialysis center, which can be time-consuming and disruptive to daily life [N2-R2][N3-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that **PD can improve mobility and flexibility** [N2-R2], while **HD patients report lower quality of life in the environment and social relationships domains** [N3-R1].

So, for practical purposes, **PD is generally less demanding in terms of travel and time** for most patients, especially those who want flexibility and independence [N2-R2][N3-R1]. However, **in-center care may still be necessary for patients who cannot manage home treatment or who require more frequent monitoring** [N2-R1][N3-R1].

### Cost and insurance coverage implications

The evidence does not provide detailed Hong Kong-specific cost or insurance figures in the provided excerpts. However, it does imply that **cost and reimbursement structures can influence access**. One source notes that **the PD-first policy was introduced to meet rising waiting list needs and because CAPD was shown to be cost-effective** [N1-F1]. Another source states that **fundamental changes are needed to the structure of medical payments and reimbursements that support vascular or peritoneal dialysis** [N4-R5]. This suggests that **reimbursement is part of the system landscape**, but the exact cost implications for patients are not clearly specified in the evidence.

In general, PD may have **different cost implications** than HD, especially because it is home-based and may reduce travel and center utilization. However, the provided evidence is not sufficient to give a precise cost comparison for Hong Kong patients [N1-F1][N4-R5].

### Local policy or system barriers to starting home dialysis

Policy barriers are clearly present. The evidence shows that **Hong Kong has a PD-first policy since 1985**, which is a major enabler, but also that **barriers to PD and the need for sustainability of the PD-first policy were emphasized** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **a critical mass of PD regional hubs is needed for training and mentorship**, and that **alignment of policy and clinical goals are enablers of the PD-first program** [N1-F1]. This implies that while the policy supports PD, it still requires ongoing support structures to function effectively.

Other barriers include the need for **patient education**, **training**, and **equipment support** [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence also suggests that **not all patients are equally suited to home dialysis**, and that **non-medical reasons are important factors in dialysis modality selection** [N5-R3]. So, the main system barriers are not necessarily a complete lack of home dialysis, but rather **training, readiness, and support limitations** that can prevent some patients from starting home treatment.

## Bottom line
In Hong Kong, **home dialysis is available and supported through a PD-first policy and training infrastructure**, but the decision is not automatic [N1-F1][N6-R2]. PD is generally more convenient in terms of travel and time, while HD requires more regular center visits [N2-R2][N3-R1]. Cost and insurance details are not fully specified in the provided evidence, but reimbursement structures do influence access and sustainability [N1-F1][N4-R5]. System barriers include the need for **training, equipment, readiness, and policy alignment**, which mean that **some patients may not be able to start home dialysis even if the policy supports it** [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-R3].

## Bottom line
In Hong Kong, **PD is more common and often a better starting option for many patients**, but it is not the right choice for everyone. The evidence supports **a shared decision-making approach** rather than a one-size-fits-all recommendation [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## Which dialysis option is better for most patients?

Overall, the evidence suggests that **peritoneal dialysis (PD) is not universally better than in-center hemodialysis (HD), but it can be more suitable for many patients depending on their circumstances**. The strongest conclusion is that **PD and in-center HD are both viable options, but neither should be chosen purely by default** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R3].

### Clinical outcomes comparison: survival, complications, and safety

The evidence indicates that **PD can offer patient survival comparable to or better than in-center HD, while preserving residual kidney function and empowering patient autonomy** [N2-R1]. That is a major advantage for long-term outcomes. However, the evidence also notes important differences in complication profiles. For frail elderly patients, **in-center HD may have advantages in efficient solute removal and limited time spent for treatment**, which is relevant for safety and tolerability in vulnerable patients [N2-R3]. 

On the safety side, the evidence is mixed. One source states that **PD is considered a preferred option particularly under pandemic conditions**, partly because of its home-based nature and reduced need for frequent center visits [N2-R1][N1-F1]. Another source notes that **home dialysis patients are generally younger and healthier than those treated with in-center HD in the US**, implying that patient selection and health status matter substantially for safety and outcomes [N2-R4]. Taken together, the evidence does **not support a single modality as universally superior**; instead, it supports the idea that **each modality has strengths and risks depending on the patient population** [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Burden and quality-of-life tradeoffs for patient lifestyle

Quality-of-life and burden considerations are a major part of the evidence. PD is associated with **greater autonomy, lower anxiety, a better relationship with medical staff, and lower pain**, according to one source [N3-R3]. Another source reports that **HD patients report lower quality of life in the environment and social relationships domains**, and more symptoms in the GHQ-28 [N3-R1]. A broader review of burden, health-related quality of life, and employment also supports the idea that PD and HD place different demands on patients and their families [N3-R2][N3-R5].

In practical terms, PD can be **more convenient for travel and mobility**, and patients on PD may experience **continuous dialysis that can improve well-being** [N2-R2]. But PD also requires home-based treatment, which may introduce burdens such as managing dialysate, catheter care, and adherence. HD, by contrast, requires regular trips to the center and more structured time commitments [N2-R2][N3-R1]. So the evidence favors **PD for patients who value flexibility, autonomy, and less disruption to daily life**, while **HD may be more appropriate for patients who prefer structured in-center care** [N2-R2][N3-R3][N3-R1].

### When each option is more suitable based on patient factors

The evidence strongly supports a **patient-centered, individualized approach** rather than a one-size-fits-all rule. A clinical guideline source emphasizes that **non-medical reasons are important factors in dialysis modality selection**, and that **the expertise of the nephrologic team is the most important one** [N5-R3]. Another source says that clinical guidelines recommend **patients' self-selection of KRT modality through shared decision-making**, which requires predialysis education and discussion [N5-R4]. A third source similarly stresses that **modality education is needed for all eligible kidney disease patients** [N5-R5].

So the best fit depends on several patient factors:
- **Age and frailty**: In frail elderly patients, in-center HD may be preferred for more efficient solute removal and less time burden [N2-R3].
- **Mobility and lifestyle**: PD may be more suitable for people who want flexibility, travel, or a more independent routine [N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **Psychosocial support**: PD may be better if the patient has family or caregiver support, whereas HD may be preferred if the patient prefers routine center care [N2-R2][N3-R1].
- **Health status and education**: HD may be more appropriate for older or less healthy patients, while PD may be better for younger, healthier patients who can manage home treatment [N2-R4].
- **Dialysis goals**: PD can preserve residual kidney function, while HD may be preferred for rapid solute clearance in some settings [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Whether evidence favors one modality overall or depends on individual circumstances

The evidence does **not favor one modality overall**. Instead, it clearly favors **individualized decision-making**. One source says that **the appropriateness of the dialysis modality selection process is important**, and that a percentage of patients could potentially have been offered a different modality [N5-R2]. Another says that **non-medical reasons are important factors**, and that **expertise of the nephrologic team is the most important one** [N5-R3]. A third says that **shared decision-making is recommended**, with predialysis education as a minimum requirement [N5-R4].

In short, the evidence supports:
- **PD as a strong first choice for many patients**, especially those who can manage home treatment and benefit from autonomy and flexibility [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **HD as a strong first choice in some patients**, especially frail or elderly patients, where in-center care may be safer or more convenient [N2-R3].
- **A decision based on the patient’s unique medical, psychosocial, and lifestyle factors**, with shared decision-making and education central to the process [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## Bottom line for most patients
The best answer is **not “choose PD” or “choose HD”**. The evidence suggests that **each modality has advantages and disadvantages**, and the better choice depends on the **patient’s age, health status, lifestyle, support system, and preferences** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-R3]. In general, **PD may be better for most patients who can manage home dialysis and value autonomy**, while **HD may be better for frail or elderly patients or those who prefer in-center care** [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-R4].

## What is the current dialysis landscape in Hong Kong?

The evidence shows that Hong Kong has a **very strong PD-first policy** and that **peritoneal dialysis is much more common than hemodialysis**. It also indicates that **home dialysis is supported in practice, but not universally accessible**, and that **local policy, training, and reimbursement structures influence patient choice** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-F2][N6-F1].

### Which dialysis modality is more common in Hong Kong

The evidence is clear: **PD is far more common than HD in Hong Kong**. One source says that **in 2013, the ratio of PD to HD was 76.2% to 23.8%**, the highest in the world [N1-R2]. Another source states that **as of 2021, 73.6% of HA dialysis patients were on PD and 26.3% on HD** [N1-F1]. A recent Renal Registry update also reports that **82.3% of new patients received PD and 17.0% received HD in 2022** [N1-F2]. So the current landscape is **PD dominant**.

### How access and support for home dialysis differ from in-center care

Home dialysis, especially PD, is supported in Hong Kong through a structured system. The evidence shows that **Hong Kong has 16 renal centres providing peritoneal dialysis treatment** and that **as of 2021, 15 centres have over 180 PD patients** [N1-R1]. It also states that **the HA has had a PD-first policy since 1985**, and that **PD was provided as the first-line dialysis regimen unless a medical contraindication dictated otherwise** [N1-F1]. This policy structure suggests that **home dialysis is integrated into the broader system**, but not automatically available to every patient.

In contrast, in-center hemodialysis remains a standard option, though less common. The evidence also notes that **the PD-first policy was introduced by the Central Renal Committee and promoted by the Hospital Authority** to meet rising waiting list needs and because CAPD was shown to be cost-effective [N1-F1]. So, access is **not equally distributed** across settings. PD is supported through a policy and training framework, while HD is still available but less emphasized in the current landscape [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Any local reimbursement or policy differences affecting patient choice

The evidence indicates that **policy differences matter**. Hong Kong has a **PD-first policy**, which is a major determinant of patient choice [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The evidence also points to **training and support structures** as important to implementation, including **home dialysis training** and **equipment support** [N6-R2][N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide a complete local reimbursement schedule in the provided excerpts, so this part is only partially supported.

That said, the broader policy context suggests that **reimbursement and reimbursement-related incentives can shape access**. The evidence notes that **home dialysis is considered a preferred option, especially under pandemic conditions**, and that **telemedicine and support structures are important adjuncts** to care [N1-F1]. Another source also says that **policy and clinical goals must align for a PD-first program to succeed**, implying that **system-level incentives are part of the landscape** [N1-F1]. Therefore, while the provided evidence is thin on exact reimbursement details, it does support the conclusion that **policy differences, including PD-first policy and training support, affect patient choice** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R2].

### How long the PD-first policy has been in place and its implementation

The evidence is very clear on this point. The PD-first policy was introduced in **Hong Kong in 1985** by the **Central Renal Committee of the Medical and Health Department** [N1-F1]. It was further promoted by the **Hospital Authority (HA)** to meet rising dialysis waiting list needs [N1-F1]. The policy was based on the idea that CAPD was cost-effective and should be provided first unless there was a medical contraindication [N1-F1].

The implementation has been long-standing and evolving. The evidence says that **starting from early 2000, representatives from Thailand and Singapore visited Hong Kong to learn PD-first experience**, and that **leading Hong Kong nephrologists have shared the policy with countries in Asia-Pacific** [N1-F1]. It also states that the **PD-first policy has been officially complimented by the U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services in 2019** as exemplary [N1-F1]. More recent data show that **the PD proportion has declined slightly from 82% in 2009 to 73.6% in 2021**, partly because of a planned increase in HD provision by the HA [N1-F1]. This indicates that the policy has been **implemented for over 35 years** and continues to evolve in practice [N1-F1][N1-F2].

## Bottom line
In Hong Kong, the current dialysis landscape is dominated by **peritoneal dialysis**, with a strong **PD-first policy that has been in place since 1985** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Access to home dialysis exists through training and support structures, but the evidence does not provide a complete reimbursement picture [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In-center hemodialysis remains available, but it is less common than PD [N1-F1]. Overall, the landscape is shaped by **policy, training, and reimbursement differences**, with PD-first policy being central to patient choice [N1-F1][N1-F2][N4-R2].

Choosing between PD and dialysis center care in Hong Kong involves four main practical considerations: **availability of home dialysis training and equipment support**, **travel and time commitments for dialysis center visits**, **cost and insurance coverage implications**, and **local policy or system barriers to starting home dialysis** [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

This indicates that **Hong Kong’s system likely supports training**, though the provided evidence does not specify whether all patients receive the same level of support.

For dialysis center care, the main burden is **travel and time**. The evidence notes that **PD is preferred under pandemic conditions because of reduced need for frequent center visits** [N2-R1][N1-F1]. In contrast, HD requires regular trips to the dialysis center, which can be time-consuming and disruptive to daily life [N2-R2][N3-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that **PD can improve mobility and flexibility** [N2-R2], while **HD patients report lower quality of life in the environment and social relationships domains** [N3-R1].

So, for practical purposes, **PD is generally less demanding in terms of travel and time** for most patients, especially those who want flexibility and independence [N2-R2][N3-R1]. ### Local policy or system barriers to starting home dialysis

Policy barriers are clearly present. The evidence shows that **Hong Kong has a PD-first policy since 1985**, which is a major enabler, but also that **barriers to PD and the need for sustainability of the PD-first policy were emphasized** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **a critical mass of PD regional hubs is needed for training and mentorship**, and that **alignment of policy and clinical goals are enablers of the PD-first program** [N1-F1]. In Hong Kong, **home dialysis is available and supported through a PD-first policy and training infrastructure**, but the decision is not automatic [N1-F1][N6-R2]. # Should I choose peritoneal dialysis or go to a dialysis center if I live in Hong Kong?

## Short answer
If you live in Hong Kong, **peritoneal dialysis (PD) is often a better starting option for many patients**, but it is not the right choice for everyone. The evidence shows that Hong Kong has a **very strong PD-first policy**, and **PD is much more common than hemodialysis (HD)** there [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R2]. However, the best choice depends on **your age, health, lifestyle, preferences, and support system**, and the evidence does not support one modality as universally “better” than the other [N2-R1][N3-R3][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## What is the dialysis landscape in Hong Kong?
Hong Kong has a long-standing **PD-first policy** that has been in place since **1985** [N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that **PD is far more common than HD**:
- In 2013, the ratio of PD to HD was **76.2% to 23.8%**, one of the highest in the world [N1-R2].
- As of 2021, **73.6% of HA dialysis patients were on PD and 26.3% on HD** [N1-F1].
- In 2022, **82.3% of new patients received PD and 17.0% received HD** [N1-F2].

Hong Kong also has **16 renal centres providing PD treatment**, and **15 centres had over 180 PD patients as of 2021** [N1-R1]. This means **home dialysis is available and supported** through a structured system, but the evidence does not give a complete reimbursement picture [N1-F1][N6-R2].

### Key practical differences
- **PD** is home-based, which can be more convenient for travel and daily life [N2-R2][N1-F1].
- **HD** requires regular trips to a dialysis center [N2-R2].
- The policy landscape, training, and support structures affect patient choice [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-R3].

## Which dialysis option is better for most patients?
Overall, the evidence suggests that **PD is not universally better than HD, but it can be more suitable for many patients depending on their circumstances** [N2-R1][N3-R3].

### Clinical outcomes: survival, complications, and safety
- **PD can offer patient survival comparable to or better than in-center HD**, while preserving residual kidney function and empowering patient autonomy [N2-R1].
- In some frail elderly patients, **in-center HD may have advantages in efficient solute removal and limited time spent for treatment** [N2-R3].
- The evidence also notes that **home dialysis patients are generally younger and healthier than those treated with in-center HD in the US**, indicating that patient selection and health status matter [N2-R4].

So, **each modality has strengths and risks depending on the patient population**, and the evidence does **not support a single modality as universally superior** [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Burden and quality-of-life tradeoffs
- PD is associated with **greater autonomy, lower anxiety, a better relationship with medical staff, and lower pain** [N3-R3].
- HD patients report **lower quality of life in the environment and social relationships domains**, and more symptoms in the GHQ-28 [N3-R1].
- A broader review of burden, health-related quality of life, and employment supports the idea that PD and HD place different demands on patients and their families [N3-R2][N3-R5].

In practical terms:
- PD can be **more convenient for travel and mobility**, and may improve well-being [N2-R2].
- HD may be preferred by patients who value routine in-center care [N3-R1].

### When each option is more suitable
The evidence strongly supports **individualized decision-making**, not a one-size-fits-all rule. A guideline source says that **non-medical reasons are important factors in dialysis modality selection**, and that **the expertise of the nephrologic team is the most important one** [N5-R3]. Another source says that **shared decision-making is recommended**, with predialysis education as a minimum requirement [N5-R4]. A third source similarly stresses that **modality education is needed for all eligible kidney disease patients** [N5-R5].

So the best fit depends on several factors:
- **Age and frailty**: In frail elderly patients, in-center HD may be preferred [N2-R3].
- **Mobility and lifestyle**: PD may be more suitable for people who want flexibility, travel, or a more independent routine [N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **Psychosocial support**: PD may be better if the patient has family or caregiver support, whereas HD may be preferred if the patient prefers routine center care [N2-R2][N3-R1].
- **Health status and education**: HD may be more appropriate for older or less healthy patients, while PD may be better for younger, healthier patients who can manage home treatment [N2-R4].
- **Dialysis goals**: PD can preserve residual kidney function, while HD may be preferred for rapid solute clearance in some settings [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Bottom line on “which is better”
The evidence does **not favor one modality overall**. Instead, it supports **a patient-centered, shared decision-making approach** [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. In general:
- **PD may be better for most patients who can manage home dialysis and value autonomy, flexibility, and less disruption to daily life** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **HD may be better for frail or elderly patients or those who prefer in-center care** [N2-R3][N5-R4].

## Practical considerations if you live in Hong Kong
If you live in Hong Kong, the choice also depends on local access, training, equipment, travel, and policy barriers.

Hong Kong has **16 renal centres providing PD treatment**, and **15 centres had over 180 PD patients as of 2021** [N1-R1]. A training source says that **before starting home dialysis, the training team checks the home, sets up the treatment space, arranges needed surgery, and provides information on dialysis** [N6-R2]. Another source says that **training programs vary in length depending on the patient’s needs** and teach patients how to safely perform dialysis, monitor health, and manage complications [N6-R5].

So, **home dialysis is available and supported**, but the level of training and support may vary [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

### Travel and time commitments
- **PD is generally less demanding in terms of travel and time** for most patients, especially if you want flexibility and independence [N2-R2][N3-R1].
- **HD requires regular trips to the dialysis center**, which can be time-consuming and disruptive [N2-R2][N3-R1].
- The evidence notes that **PD is preferred under pandemic conditions because of reduced need for frequent center visits** [N2-R1][N1-F1].

### Cost and insurance coverage implications
The evidence does **not provide a complete Hong Kong-specific cost or insurance picture**, but it does imply that **cost and reimbursement structures can influence access** [N1-F1][N4-R5]. One source notes that **the PD-first policy was introduced to meet rising waiting list needs and because CAPD was shown to be cost-effective** [N1-F1]. Another source says that **fundamental changes are needed to the structure of medical payments and reimbursements that support vascular or peritoneal dialysis** [N4-R5].

So, while the evidence does not give exact costs, it supports the idea that **reimbursement and payment structures matter for access and sustainability** [N1-F1][N4-R5].

### Local policy or system barriers
Policy barriers are clearly present:
- Hong Kong has a **PD-first policy since 1985**, which is a major enabler [N1-F1].
- The evidence also emphasizes **barriers to PD and the need for sustainability of the PD-first policy** [N1-F1].
- It notes that **a critical mass of PD regional hubs is needed for training and mentorship**, and that **policy and clinical goals must align** for the program to succeed [N1-F1].

This means that while the policy supports PD, it still requires ongoing training, support, and readiness to function effectively. Some patients may not be able to start home dialysis even if the policy supports it [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-R3].

## Final recommendation
If you live in Hong Kong, the best answer is:
- **Start with PD if you can manage home dialysis and prefer autonomy, flexibility, and less disruption to your daily life** [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R3].
- **Consider HD if you are frail, elderly, or prefer routine in-center care** [N2-R3][N3-R1].
- **Choose based on your individual situation**, including age, health, lifestyle, support system, and preferences [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## Bottom line
In Hong Kong, **PD is more common and often a better starting option for many patients**, but it is not the right choice for everyone. The evidence supports **a shared decision-making approach** rather than a one-size-fits-all recommendation [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4].
